newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik govt troops reach abandoned rebel stronghold.
newsitem.headline: Tajik govt troops reach abandoned rebel stronghold.

text.p: Government troops on Tuesday entered the former rebel stronghold of Kabodien in southern Tajikistan after it was abandoned by mutinous Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev and his men.
A Reuter correspondent said only sporadic shooting was heard but reported no major fighting in the town, which lies 160 km (100 miles) southwest of the capital Dushanbe.
The troops were also preparing to advance on the rebel-held town of Shaartuz, 20 km (12 miles) south of Kabodien, a government military source said.

Shaartuz is only a short distance from the Tajik border with Afghanistan and the former Soviet republic of Uzbekistan and is the last stronghold of Khudoyberdyev, whose men have been pulling back since their rebellion ended last Wednesday.

On Monday Interfax news agency quoted the head of the presidential guard, General Gafar Mirzoyev, as saying government troops had encircled Khudoyberdyev's units, which numbered about 1,400 men, three tanks and several armoured personnel carriers.

He said Khudoyberdyev's only option was to lay down his arms because it would be very difficult for him to cross the Tajik border. Mirzoyev said that Khudoyberdyev's men were using Grad multiple missile launchers and artillery against his troops.

The latest turmoil to rock the impoverished former Soviet republic began with clashes in Dushanbe between competing warlords and presidential forces on August 9 and Khudoyberdyev began moving his brigade towards the capital.

It came just weeks after Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, who is backed by Moscow, signed a peace accord with Islamic opposition guerrillas aimed at ending four years of civil war. The Islamic guerrillas were not involved in the latest clashes.
Khudoyberdyev began pulling his troops back on Wednesday after losing a strategic aluminium-producing town west of Dushanbe to presidential forces.
His deputy, Lieutenant-Colonel Sergei Zavarygin, told Reuters on Saturday that Khudoyberdyev and his men would not surrender their weapons but would "fight to the bitter end".
